summary: Defines a BGP capability that lets a speaker send its peer a set of Outbound Route Filters. The peer then applies those filters to limit which routes it sends back. This moves filtering to the sender, reducing the number of routing updates a router has to receive and discard, and it is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of receiving all the junk mail and throwing it out, you give the post office a list of what you want. Then it only sends the right letters.

questions: how to filter routes at the sender in bgp
what is bgp outbound route filtering
how does bgp route refresh carry orf entries
subtitle: How a BGP router can tell its neighbor which routes it wants, so unwanted ones are never sent.

tldr.problem: A BGP speaker often receives routes from a peer and then throws some away under its local policy. Generating, sending and processing those unwanted updates wastes resources on both sides.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver sends its peer a set of Outbound Route Filters (ORFs) inside a BGP ROUTE-REFRESH message, after both sides agree on it using a new BGP capability (code 3). The peer applies those filters to what it sends back.
tldr.outcome: Filtering moves to the sender, which can avoid generating unwanted updates in the first place. The filters are a request that the peer may or may not honor, and they last only for the BGP session.

today: RFC 5291 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the capability and the common ORF format; specific ORF types are registered separately with IANA.

sections.title: Filtering Before the Update Is Sent
sections.content:
It is common for a BGP speaker to receive routes from a peer and then filter some of them out under its local routing policy. The sender still had to generate and transmit those updates, and the receiver still had to process them, so the work was wasted.

RFC 5291 defines a way for a speaker to send its peer a set of Outbound Route Filters (ORFs). The peer applies them, in addition to any outbound filters it has configured locally, to limit the routing updates it sends back.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine telling your friend which stickers you want before they bring any, instead of taking all of them and giving back the ones you do not like.

sections.title: What an ORF Entry Contains
sections.content:
Conceptually an ORF entry is a tuple of AFI/SAFI, ORF-Type, Action, Match and ORF-value. An ORF is a group of entries sharing the same AFI/SAFI and ORF-Type, and it is identified by that pair.

  • The AFI/SAFI limits the ORF to routes of that address family.
  • The ORF-Type decides what the ORF-value looks like.
  • The Action is ADD, REMOVE or REMOVE-ALL. ADD adds an entry on the remote peer, REMOVE deletes one, and REMOVE-ALL deletes every entry in the specified ORF.
  • The Match is PERMIT (pass updates for routes matching the entry) or DENY (do not pass them).

Whenever an ORF type is defined, it MUST come with a matching rule, so it is never ambiguous which entry applies to a route.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry is one line on your wish list: which kind of thing, whether to add or cross it off, and whether you want it or do not want it.

sections.title: Carrying ORFs in ROUTE-REFRESH
sections.content:
ORF entries ride in the BGP ROUTE-REFRESH message. A receiver tells a plain ROUTE-REFRESH from one carrying ORF entries by the Message Length field in the BGP message header. One message MAY carry many entries in one or more ORFs, as long as they all share the same AFI/SAFI.

After the AFI and SAFI comes a one-octet When-to-refresh field, IMMEDIATE (0x01) or DEFER (0x02). Then come groups of entries, each group made of a one-octet ORF Type, a two-octet length of the entries that follow, and the entries themselves.

In the first octet of each entry, Action takes two bits (0 for ADD, 1 for REMOVE, 2 for REMOVE-ALL), Match takes one bit (0 for PERMIT, 1 for DENY, significant only for ADD or REMOVE) and five reserved bits are set to 0 and ignored on receipt. A REMOVE-ALL entry consists of only this common part.
sections.plainLanguage: The wish list goes inside a note that already exists for asking for a resend. A small label on the note says if the sender should act now or wait.

sections.title: The ORF Capability
sections.content:
A speaker that wants to receive ORFs, send ORFs, or both advertises the new Outbound Route Filtering Capability, which is BGP capability code 3 with a variable length. Its value lists, for an AFI/SAFI, a number of ORF types, and for each type a Send/Receive value: 1 means willing to receive ORF entries from the peer, 2 means would like to send them, and 3 means both.

A speaker MAY send ORF entries only if it advertised that it wants to send, the peer advertised that it is willing to receive, and the entries use an AFI/SAFI and ORF type the peer agreed to receive.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending a wish list, each side says whether it can send lists, read lists, or both. Lists only go where someone agreed to read them.

sections.title: How Peers Apply Filters
sections.content:
A speaker implementing this capability MUST support the ROUTE-REFRESH message from RFC 2918. If the two sides' advertised sets overlap for an AFI/SAFI, the filtered speaker SHOULD NOT advertise routes of that AFI/SAFI until it gets a ROUTE-REFRESH for it, either without ORF entries or with entries and When-to-refresh set to IMMEDIATE. If they do not overlap, normal BGP procedures apply.

On receipt, entries for an AFI/SAFI and type that was not agreed are ignored. Otherwise the stored ORF is modified. An unrecognized value in any field removes the whole ORF received so far, and a REMOVE for an entry that is not there is ignored. REMOVE and REMOVE-ALL cannot remove locally configured outbound filters.

With IMMEDIATE, the speaker re-advertises routes from the Adj-RIB-Out for that AFI/SAFI, taking the ORF entries into account; it MUST re-advertise all routes affected and MAY re-advertise others. With DEFER, it waits until a later ROUTE-REFRESH without ORF entries, or with IMMEDIATE, arrives for that AFI/SAFI.

A route that matches no entry of any non-empty ORF for the peer SHOULD NOT be advertised. With several ORF types for a peer, the route passes through each, and combining PERMIT with DENY gives DENY. The entries express the sender's preference, which the peer may or may not honor. An ORF lasts for the BGP session and is removed when its last entry is removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper reads your list and only sends the matching letters. If something is on both a yes list and a no list, no wins.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Manageability
sections.content:
The ORF capability gets Capability Code 3. IANA maintains a registry named "BGP Outbound Route Filtering (ORF) Types" for the ORF-Type field: value 0 is reserved; 1 through 63 are assigned by Standards Action (RFC 5226) or Early IANA Allocation (RFC 4020); 64 through 127 are First Come First Served; 128 through 255 are vendor-specific and not assigned by IANA.

Management objects are to be defined outside this document. It suggests an ORF Capability object recording the types and Send/Receive values advertised and received, and an ORF entry object holding the entries sent and received per peer.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of the kinds of wish lists, and some number ranges are kept free for companies to use however they like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is one sentence: this extension to BGP does not change the underlying security issues of BGP-4.
sections.plainLanguage: This idea does not make the old safety problems better or worse.

fields.name: ORF Type
fields.desc: Type of the entries that follow.

fields.name: Length of ORF entries
fields.desc: Total length in octets of the entries that follow for this type.

viz.caption: SEND/RECEIVE VALUES IN THE ORF CAPABILITY

items.label: Receive
items.desc: Willing to receive ORF entries from the peer.

items.label: Send
items.desc: Would like to send ORF entries to the peer.

items.label: Both
items.desc: Both willing to receive and wanting to send.
